idiom_name: case [a, b] when [Circle, Square] (Module#=== applied element-wise)
implementation_notes: Ruby dispatches on the receiver only and has no method overloading, so the everyday replacement for the classic round-trip is a case over the pair: `case [a, b] when [Circle, Square]` works because case compares with Array#===, which applies Module#=== (an is_a? test) to each element. The whole matrix stays readable in one place, which is the closest Ruby comes to pattern matching without the newer `in` syntax; the Beck-style round-trip (see visitor-round-trip) is still the choice when both hierarchies are open or third parties must add types.
code_sketch:
def collide(a, b)
  case [a, b]
  when [Circle, Square] then "circle #{a.radius} vs square #{b.side}"
  when [Square, Circle] then collide(b, a)      # canonicalise symmetric pairs
  when [Circle, Circle] then "two circles"
  else raise ArgumentError, "unhandled pair #{a.class}/#{b.class}"
  end
end
pitfalls: Without an else branch an unhandled pair returns nil silently: raise from the else branch.
Module#=== is an is_a? test, so a subclass matches its parent's arm and arm order becomes semantics.
case on an array allocates one array per call; in hot paths dispatch on a precomputed key instead.

variants.name: Send a message to the argument (Beck's form)
variants.idiom_name: medium.render_circle(self) - receiver's class name appended to the selector
variants.implementation_notes: Beck's Smalltalk pattern, which Ruby inherits directly: the receiver sends a message to the argument, appending its own class name to the selector (medium.render_circle(self)), so the second dispatch - on the argument's runtime type - resolves against the receiver's concrete type. Ruby's unrestricted dynamic dispatch makes this cheap and open to new types, at the price of scattering the receiver's type names over every collaborator; the generated-selector variation send("visit_#{other.class}") is common but refactor-hostile. Ruby's standard library contains a built-in instance of the same shape for operators: Numeric#coerce returns the two operands rewritten into a common type when the left operand cannot handle the right.
variants.code_sketch:
class Circle
  def collide_with(other)
    other.collide_circle(self)      # dispatch #2: argument's type picks the method
  end
end

class Square
  def collide_circle(circle)
    "circle #{circle.radius} vs square #{side}"
  end
end
pitfalls: String-built selectors (send("visit_#{other.class}")) are slow, invisible to refactoring tools and unsafe when the name can be influenced by input.
Every collaborator must know every receiver type by name, so adding a shape means editing every medium.
coerce only covers numeric protocols and must return the rewritten pair; forgetting the reflected case raises TypeError on the reversed operand order.
